caption:
The University of California is paying OpenAI $1.2 million for a one-year deal that gives ChatGPT Edu to all 10 campuses, starting in December.
That covers about 300,000 students. Cal State paid $39 million for three years.
The faculty Senate asked UC to wait and called universal access "unwise." The president went ahead anyway.

Should every college student get ChatGPT for free?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Sacramento Bee, EdSource · Photo: Sacramento Bee
threads_text: The University of California just bought ChatGPT Edu for about 300,000 students for $1.2 million a year. Cal State paid $39 million for three years. UC's own faculty Senate called universal access unwise and asked it to wait. Good deal or bad idea?

site_article.seo_title: UC signs $1.2M OpenAI deal for ChatGPT Edu on all campuses
site_article.seo_description: The University of California will pay OpenAI $1.2 million for ChatGPT Edu on all 10 campuses from December, over objections from its faculty Senate.
site_article.answer_summary: The University of California is paying OpenAI $1.2 million for one year of ChatGPT Edu and Codex access for its roughly 300,000 students and its staff and faculty, starting in December 2026.

paragraphs.text: The University of California has signed a $1.2 million agreement with OpenAI that gives ChatGPT Edu to students, staff and faculty across its 10 campuses, according to the Sacramento Bee. The one-year deal starts on December 1, 2026, and also includes access to Codex, OpenAI's coding agent, along with expanded workforce training and AI literacy workshops.

The system enrolls about 300,000 students and employs about 265,000 workers, the Sacramento Bee reported. EdSource, in a story republished by LAist, described the agreement as a one-year partnership that extends an earlier contract with OpenAI.
How the deal grew out of a 2024 contract

UC first signed a systemwide agreement with OpenAI for ChatGPT Enterprise and Edu in June 2024. According to the UC Office of the President's procurement page, that contract had a three-year term with two one-year renewal options, and included confidentiality protections for prompts and responses. Under it, individual campuses could buy OpenAI services as needed, but the arrangement did not give access to every campus.

UC chief information officer Van Williams told the Sacramento Bee that the university owns the data in its licensed ChatGPT accounts, that OpenAI cannot reshare, monetize or retain it, and that the federal student privacy law FERPA applies. In an October email to the Academic Senate chair, cited by EdSource, Williams described the negotiation as a chance to lower costs, strengthen enterprise protections and widen access, and said the university had to move quickly.
A lower price than Cal State

The price is far below what California State University has paid. The Sacramento Bee reported that CSU signed a $17 million, 18-month contract with OpenAI in January 2025 and renewed it in July 2026 for $39 million over three years, covering about 470,000 students and 63,000 workers on 22 campuses. Williams told the paper that UC was not going to pay what CSU paid, that it negotiated hard and that it raised the option of choosing Anthropic. Talks with Anthropic are continuing, and UC also has agreements with Google and Microsoft, the paper said.

The faculty Academic Senate asked the university to put off the purchase. In an October 30 letter to UC President James Milliken, Senate chair Susannah Scott cited shared governance and very limited consultation, and described the decision as more than a routine software purchase. According to EdSource, the Senate said it is unwise to give every student a tool that can perform the academic work required for a degree before faculty concerns about curriculum, teaching and academic integrity are addressed.

The Sacramento Bee reported that the Senate was told about the purchase roughly 10 days before it was finalized, and that the item was on the Academic Council's November 19 agenda after the decision had already been made. Scott told EdSource that the core concerns in the October letter remain unresolved. The Senate did not object to the use of AI itself, according to the Bee, but some faculty worried that universal access would look like an endorsement of ChatGPT in every course.

Milliken replied that providing the tools does not require anyone to use them, and wrote that the decision has the full support of all UC chancellors. A UC spokesperson told EdSource that administrators had discussed the partnership with Senate leaders and faculty since the spring.

The agreement shows how quickly price has fallen for universities that buy AI tools at scale, and how much leverage a large system gains when several AI companies want its students. The dispute with faculty is less about whether AI belongs on campus and more about who decides how it is used in teaching.

Access begins in December, so the next signal is whether individual campuses and departments set their own rules for ChatGPT in coursework, and whether UC adds Anthropic or other providers under the talks it describes as ongoing.
